The invisibility cloak is designed using a linear homogeneous transformation method, which avoids the need for extreme and spatially dependent material parameters required in previous transformation optics-based cloak designs.
The simplified hexagonal cloak fabricated for experimental demonstration had an inner radius of 1.5 mm and an outer radius of 13 cm, with a height of 13 mm.
The simplified hexagonal cloak was fabricated using six calcite trapezoids glued together, with the optic axis in each trapezoid parallel to its sides.
The hidden object concealed by the cloak was a 1.3 mm radius yellow column.

The cloak was able to guide a red laser beam incident normally on the hidden column around it without any deviation, as well as guide two green laser beams incident at oblique angles around the column.
Due to fabrication errors, the outer radius and height of the fabricated cloak had an error up to 1 mm, and the gap between the glued pieces had an error up to 0.3 mm.
The simplified hexagonal cloak can only work for rays incident from six directions, while the theoretically proposed polygonal cloak can work for rays incident from all directions.
The linear homogeneous transformation method used in this cloak design can be useful for designing different shaped cloaks and other optical devices beyond just invisibility cloaks.

A key challenge in scaling invisibility cloak designs from microwave to visible light frequencies is placing sub-wavelength resonant metamaterial elements in a spatially dependent manner at optical frequencies.

The authors validated the cloak's performance by demonstrating its ability to guide laser beams of different colors and incident angles around the hidden object without distortion, as well as by capturing images showing the hidden object was concealed from view.

The simplified hexagonal cloak was fabricated by replacing the highly anisotropic Segment I materials in the original polygonal cloak design with the more isotropic Segment II materials, sacrificing some performance but allowing the use of natural birefringent crystals like calcite.

The first experimental demonstration of a cylindrical invisibility cloak was reported in 2006 at microwave frequencies, but the operating frequency of isolated invisibility cloaks has remained in the microwave frequencies until this work.

The transformation optics-based cloak design can achieve broadband, omni-directional cloaking without requiring extreme or singular material parameters, making it more feasible to implement experimentally compared to previous proposals.
The authors used a ray tracing model to demonstrate the path of the rays inside the cloak, verifying the performance of the cloak in manipulating the incident light.

The simplified hexagonal cloak fabricated for experimental demonstration sacrificed some of the performance of the original polygonal cloak design, but was still able to successfully conceal the hidden object.
